visual_anchors.morphology_description: Tall cylindrical vessel with a flat green cap/lid at the top. The body is painted red-orange with two or three white horizontal decorative bands (possibly indicating measurement graduations or decorative banding typical of apothecary jars). No visible liquid level inside — contents likely dry powder or solid material. This is the primary pharmaceutical anchor for the top label group.
Small plant with 3–4 arrow/spade-shaped opposite leaves on a thin stem. Root is a thin curling tendril in brown ink, not bulbous. Leaves have visible veining. Smallest plant in the top register.

The most morphologically distinctive plant on the page. A circular coiled or spiral rhizome/tuber in orange-brown ink forms the center of the illustration. From this coil, multiple arrow-pointed green leaves radiate outward in different directions like a starburst. Root tendrils extend below the coil. The spiral morphology may encode a specific preparation method (distillation cycle, coiling = repeated processing). Acts as the bisecting object for locus <f100r.5,@Lf>.

The tallest plant in the top register. Central large triangular/conical dark green leaf cluster with serrated margins. Two lateral lobed leaves at mid-height. Orange-brown root system below. The dark green pigment (more saturated than other plants) may indicate semantic differentiation.

Upper-right plant with three lobed/palmate green leaves. Two or three of the leaf tips or small buds are painted with distinctive blue pigment — the only blue botanical element on this folio. Blue tip morphology could encode flowering state, medicinal property, or toxic marker. Root is orange-brown fibrous.
Far right upper plant. Two large, broad, rounded leaves with clearly painted venation. Orange-brown root. A separate label 'sofag' appears to the right of this plant.
Small plant left of center in the middle register. Three lobed green leaves with a thin curling brown root. Compact form.

Distinctive plant with a circular corona/sun-halo motif at the crown-root junction — a ring of short radiating strokes in orange-brown ink resembling a sun or crown. Above: green lobed leaves. Below: orange-brown root. The corona morphology is unique among visible plants and likely encodes a special preparation state (heating/drying/solar process?).

Central middle plant with a conical dark green leaf mass and a prominent elongated root tuber painted in dark red-brown — darker and more saturated than other roots. The root has a pointed distal end and a slight reddish hue distinct from the orange-brown roots elsewhere. This darker root color may semantically indicate a different root state (dried, resinous, or specific species marker).
Right-center bushy plant. Multiple rounded green leaf clusters growing from a shared crown. Orange-brown fibrous root.
Largest plant in the middle register. Two very large, broad, deeply-lobed leaves with heavy venation. Orange-brown root with multiple branching tendrils.

Second pharmaceutical jar, morphologically identical to pharma_jar_top_left: cylindrical, red-orange body with white horizontal bands, green flat lid. Positioned left margin of the lower illustration register. The repetition of an identical jar type in both registers strongly suggests a consistent recipe/formula notation system where the jar = same ingredient or preparation vessel type.
Narrow plant with elongated, slightly serrated leaves. Thin root. Positioned to the right of pharma_jar_mid_left.
Compact rounded bushy plant, dome-shaped leaf mass. Brown root with short tendrils. Smaller of the two central lower plants.

Slightly larger rounded bushy plant, similar morphology to plant_lower_center_left_round. Dense leaf cluster, short brown root. These two similar rounded plants side-by-side may represent related species or dosage variants.

The largest plant in the lower register. Multiple large, broad, serrated green leaves arranged in a loose rosette. The root system is the most elaborate on the folio: orange-brown, multi-branching, with 4–5 distinct root arms radiating downward and sideways. Root branching morphology resembles a hand/claw form. Likely indicates a multi-root medicinal plant (e.g., valerian or mandrake type).
